l: Iolaus's rejuvenation, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Iolaus prays to Juno and Jupiter to become young for one day and take vengeance on his enemies. Two stars and a dim cloud conceal the chariot, and he emerges with the appearance and arms of a young man.

l: capture of Eurystheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Iolaus seizes Eurystheus's four-horse chariot at the Scironian rocks and binds Eurystheus in fetters. Eurystheus is then brought alive before Alcmena.

l: death of Eurystheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Alcmena declares that Eurystheus must die for his many wrongs and orders the servants to kill him. His death is ordered at the end of the unit, but the text does not narrate its completion.

l: prophecy concerning Eurystheus's tomb, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: foretells Eurystheus's tomb [before the temple of the virgin of Pallene] Eurystheus says that Apollo has ordained that he be buried near the temple of the divine virgin of Pallene. From beneath the earth, he will protect Athens while becoming hostile to the descendants of those who attack the city.

l: Athenian law against executing captured enemies, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: forbids death of Eurystheus [because he was captured alive] The leaders of Athens hold that an enemy captured alive must not be put to death. Eurystheus says that killing him would bring pollution under the laws of the Greeks, and the messenger says that the city has released him for this reason.

l: divine justice and fortune, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: changes Eurystheus's fortune [from prosperity to defeat] The servant says that Eurystheus's reversal of fortune shows that mortals should not envy anyone who appears prosperous until that person is dead. The Chorus presents the victory as evidence that the gods humble the arrogance of the unjust and bring unexpected good fortune.

l: Eurystheus's tomb, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: is_a place of protection [for Athens after Eurystheus's death] Eurystheus's tomb is to be located near the temple of the divine virgin of Pallene. He says that the tomb will benefit Athens and harm the descendants of its future enemies, and he forbids libations and blood offerings there.

l: oracle, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: requires sacrifice of Macaria [one descendant of Hercules must be devoted] The oracle expressly required that one of the descendants of Hercules should be devoted.

l: old man (in Iphigenia in Aulis), The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The Old Man is a faithful slave and servant of Clytaemnestra’s household, also loyal to Agamemnon’s house, though opposed to Agamemnon. Carrying Agamemnon’s sealed warning letter to Argos, he is intercepted, robbed, and threatened by Menelaus. Knowing Iphigenia’s intended sacrifice through the letter, he later reveals Agamemnon’s plan and the failed warning to Achilles.

l: Calchas, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Calchas is a seer and prophet of the Greek army. He declares that the Greeks can sail to Troy and sack it only if Iphigenia is sacrificed to Diana, and he knows the truth about Agamemnon’s supposed marriage arrangement. His prophecy causes Agamemnon to fear disclosure and seek his counsel.

l: Myrmidons, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Led by Achilles with fifty ships at the fleet’s right horn, they stay by Euripus, urging action against Troy or return home, wind-delayed.

l: Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Aulis is a Greek harbor and the setting of the Greek expedition against Troy. The Greek army and fleet gather there: ships fill its narrow harbors, while soldiers occupy Diana’s grove, flowery meads, and tents. Separated from Euripus by a narrow strait, it is marked by stillness: the Euripus is silent and calm, the winds fail, and the fleet cannot sail. This detention becomes bound to Iphigenia. She is brought to Aulis under the pretense of marriage to Achilles, while Agamemnon plans her sacrifice so that the ships may depart. At Diana’s altar, the sacrifice is prepared; accounts describe Iphigenia as threatened, intended or attempted to be sacrificed, and nearly killed like a calf. Calchas declares that the army should leave Aulis and cross the Ægean once this condition is met. In later recollection, Aulis gains fame through the intended sacrifice, though Iphigenia is said to have been conveyed away from it. Thus Aulis unfolds from a crowded but windbound military harbor into the place of Iphigenia’s danger and the expedition’s hoped-for release toward Troy.

l: Euripus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: separates Aulis [by a narrow strait] The Euripus is the place where Achilles and the Greek forces are waiting. Its light or chilly winds delay the expedition's departure.

l: the Greek expedition against Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The Greek expedition against Troy is a Greek military campaign organized after Menelaus invokes the oath of Helen’s suitors. Waged against Troy and the Phrygians, it seeks to recover and avenge Helen for Menelaus, stop the abduction of wives, and defend Greece. Agamemnon is chosen as general, and a thousand ships assemble, drawing men from across Greece who leave their families behind. At Aulis, however, unfavorable winds at the Euripus prevent departure. The expedition’s progress becomes conditional on Iphigenia’s sacrifice: Iphigenia believes it will let the army sail, attack and destroy Troy, and gain lasting victory.

l: Iphigenia’s sacrifice at Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Iphigenia’s sacrifice at Aulis is an intended human offering to Diana, required by Calchas’s prophecy or oracle so that the Greek fleet may sail, the expedition may proceed to Troy and capture it, and Greece may gain freedom from barbarian rule. Agamemnon, compelled by this necessity, initially agrees and summons Iphigenia to Aulis under the false pretense of a marriage to Achilles. He later regrets the decision and tries to cancel it, while Menelaus wants it carried out. Clytemnestra, Iphigenia, and Achilles oppose the plan; Achilles says he will prevent it if possible, although many Greeks support it. Iphigenia is brought to the altar of Diana amid wedding-like preparations, including baths, hair, songs, garlands, baskets, purifying cakes, and lustral water. After pleading and lamentation, she accepts the offering willingly for Greece and calls for the sacrificial rites. At the altar, Agamemnon believes he has sacrificed her, and the sound of the blow is heard. Yet Iphigenia is no longer present: Diana substitutes a stag and carries Iphigenia away. Thus the rite is completed through the stag, while later accounts treat Iphigenia’s death as only supposed and recall her near-sacrifice at Aulis rather than an accomplished death.

l: Iphigenia's supposed marriage to Achilles, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Iphigenia’s supposed marriage to Achilles is a deceptive marriage rite invented by Agamemnon to bring Iphigenia and Clytaemnestra to Aulis. Publicly, Iphigenia is presented as Achilles’ bride, prompting Clytaemnestra to bring dower-gifts and seek details of the ceremony. Achilles and Clytaemnestra initially do not know that the marriage is only a pretext. The Old Man’s revelation exposes that Agamemnon has connected the supposed wedding with Iphigenia’s intended sacrifice and death. The failed marriage leaves Iphigenia ashamed, while Achilles says Agamemnon had promised her as his bride. Its language also joins preliminary marriage rites with sacrificial rites.

l: calm at Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: A calm prevents the Greeks from sailing from Aulis. The silence of the winds and sea is observed at night, and the army demands that the ships either be dismissed or continue seeking a way to depart.

l: Agamemnon's letter, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Agamemnon’s letter first summoned Iphigenia to Aulis as though she were to marry Achilles, but he writes a new letter ordering Clytaemnestra not to send her and to postpone the marriage. Menelaus breaks the seal and uses the letter to confront Agamemnon.

l: leadership and popular opinion, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Agamemnon says that honor and popular opinion are uncertain burdens for leaders. Menelaus accuses him of seeking popularity before becoming leader and then becoming difficult to approach after gaining command of the Greek army.

l: marriage and infidelity, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Helen’s departure with Paris is treated as the cause of the Greek expedition against Troy. Agamemnon condemns Menelaus for seeking to recover a wife he had failed to govern well, while Menelaus relies on the oath made by Helen’s suitors.

l: Messenger, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The Messenger announces to Agamemnon that Clytaemnestra, Iphigenia, and Orestes have arrived. He reports that the Greek army is gathering to see Iphigenia and assumes that her arrival concerns a marriage or initiation in honor of Artemis.

l: altar, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Diana’s altar is a memorial for Iphigenia and the focal place of sacrifice: at Aulis she is told she will stand by it as preparations and songs proceed; at Diana’s temple it is marked by slain strangers’ blood while Iphigenia prepares sacrifices and others kill within the shrine.

l: prophecy concerning Iphigenia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The prophecy, interpreted by Calchas, declares that Iphigenia must be sacrificed to Diana so the Greek army can sail. It threatens to expose Agamemnon’s promise and prompts his fear. Achilles distrusts such prophecy, though the chorus recalls prophecies about his Trojan role.

l: Paris and Helen's union, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: causes Trojan War Paris and Helen's union is blamed for bringing the Greeks against Troy. The Chorus portrays Paris's desire for Helen and the resulting war as the source of extensive suffering.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Chorus is a group of singers commenting on the sacrifice. It calls Iphigenia’s choice glorious while lamenting the fortune and divine forces behind the deed, prepares to sing to Diana, and describes her garlanded and purified approach to the altar. Its final part contains Nereids; several passages are corrupt, incomplete, difficult, or spurious.

l: Taurian attendants, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Taurian attendants are portrayed as slavish barbarians, feared to harm or carry off Greek women; Iphigenia opposes their rule over free Greeks.

l: lustral waters, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Iphigenia is expected to prepare lustral water and consecrations for the two captured Greek strangers before their sacrifice.

l: Iphigenia's renown, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: is_based_on Greece's freedom from barbarian rule [as her lasting glory] Iphigenia expects lasting renown from freeing Greece and enabling the destruction of Troy. She says that her sacrifice will become her memorial, while the Chorus agrees that renown will not fail her.

l: Greece's freedom from barbarian rule, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Greece's freedom from barbarian rule is presented as a justification for Iphigenia's death. She declares that Greeks should rule barbarians rather than barbarians rule Greeks, because the Greeks are free.

l: messenger (in Iphigenia in Aulis), The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: reports_on Iphigenia [to Clytæmnestra] The Messenger recounts to Clytæmnestra everything he witnessed at the grove and altar of Diana. He reports that the girl disappeared at the moment of the blow and that a stag appeared in her place.

l: Iphigenia's substitution by a hind, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Iphigenia's substitution by a hind is Artemis's exchange of a hind for Iphigenia at Diana's altar. At the sacrifice, Iphigenia vanishes; Agamemnon believes he strikes her, while a large stag or hind appears, is identified by Calchas as the Goddess's victim, and is sacrificed in her place.

l: departure of the Greek fleet, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: After the stag is reduced to ashes, Calchas prays for the army's passage. He instructs the sailors to take courage and leave Aulis to cross the Ægean, while Agamemnon says that the army is looking toward setting sail.

l: altar of Diana, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: is_wetted_with stag [with the stag's blood] The altar of Diana is the place where the girl is to be sacrificed and where the stag appears in her place. The stag's blood abundantly wets the altar, and the victim is afterward reduced to ashes.

l: sacrificial stag, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: A large, beautiful mountain-roaming stag provided by Diana appears as Iphigenia vanishes at Aulis, preferred to her as a sacrificial victim. Given to the Greeks in her place, its blood is used in the sacrifice before it is burned to ashes.

l: The Cambridge editor, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The Cambridge editor is a textual critic of Iphigenia in Aulis and Iphigenia in Tauris. The editor’s central work is proposing and supporting emendations, omissions, rearrangements, restorations, and explanations of difficult passages. The editor strongly condemns the final scene of Iphigenia in Aulis, suspects interpolations, and is often praised for judgment, taste, and choral treatment despite some rejected suggestions.

l: Iphigenia in Aulis Cambridge edition, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: is_a critical edition [of Iphigenia in Aulis] The Cambridge edition is used throughout as a major authority for textual readings, metrical analysis, interpretation, and the assignment or rejection of lines. It is particularly important for discussions of corrupt choruses, the final scene, and the play’s inconsistencies.

l: textual criticism of Iphigenia in Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Textual criticism of Iphigenia in Aulis records widespread corruption, interpolations, and disputed readings, moving through conjectures, deletions, restorations, speaker changes, and editorial judgments, especially questioning the last scene.

l: Thoas, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Thoas is the swift-footed, superstitious barbarian king who rules Tauris and Tauri. He receives two captured Greek strangers, orders them purified and guarded on Iphigenia’s account, and regards her actions as divinely guided. When Iphigenia and Orestes escape, he orders pursuit, but obeys Minerva’s command to stop and permits them and the Grecian women to depart.

l: Herdsman, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: reports arrival of Orestes and Pylades [to Iphigenia] The Herdsman reports to Iphigenia that two Greek youths have arrived at the Symplegades. He describes Orestes' madness, the attack on the cattle, the struggle with the herdsmen, and the capture of both strangers.

l: Tauris, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Tauris is an inhospitable barbarian land ruled by Thoas, containing Artemis or Diana’s temple, its sacred image, and rites in which Greeks are sacrificed. Iphigenia lives there as the goddess’s priestess. Orestes and Pylades arrive seeking the image, and Orestes is threatened with sacrifice. Iphigenia first seeks to send Pylades away and asks Orestes to take her from the land; after recognizing and joining with Orestes, she plans an escape by ship with him and the image. Thoas orders pursuit when Iphigenia, Orestes, the image, and the Grecian women flee, but Minerva stops him and allows them to depart.

l: temple of Artemis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The temple of Diana in Tauris is a sacred place containing an altar where Greek blood is shed and the image Orestes is commanded to take. Orestes and Pylades observe it, consider hiding nearby, and are brought there for rites prepared by Iphigenia, its gatekeeper and sacrificial priestess. She orders their release and sacrificial preparations, then plans to remove the image under a claim of purification from the strangers’ pollution, despite sacred keepers. Minerva finally directs that the image be taken to Athens and assigns Iphigenia to guard the Goddess’s temple at Brauron.

l: sea-coast, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The sea-coast near the Symplegades is where the herdsmen take their cattle and discover Orestes and Pylades. It is also the area from which the strangers' ship has approached.

l: Diana's image, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Diana's sacred image, said to have fallen from heaven, belongs to Artemis and stands in the Tauric temple. When strangers approach, it turns away and closes its eyes, prompting Iphigenia to remove it under pretense of purification. Orestes and Iphigenia carry it to a Grecian ship; by Phœbus's and Minerva's commands, it is taken and enshrined at Athens.

l: ship, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The ship is the vessel that brings Orestes and Pylades from Argos to Tauris after a dangerous voyage and appears near the Symplegades. It waits secretly at anchor, well-rowed and prepared for Iphigenia’s escape plan. Iphigenia, expected to end her slavery, boards it with Orestes, Pylades, and the sacred image of Artemis. As Thoas’s men attempt to stop the departure, the sailors resist. Strong currents first drive the ship back, but Minerva’s command makes it safe, and it voyages toward Greece and Athens under her protection.

l: arrival of Orestes and Pylades, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Orestes and Pylades arrive in Tauri by ship from Argos to obtain Diana's image. Their arrival is discovered by herdsmen, who capture them after a violent struggle.

l: dream of Iphigenia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Iphigenia dreams that her ancestral house collapses, leaving one pillar with golden hair and a human voice. She interprets the pillar as Orestes and concludes that her brother is dead, so she prepares funeral offerings for him.

l: Tauric festival sacrifice, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: A religious rite in Tauri/Tauris publicly offers Greek strangers to Diana/Artemis. Captured Greeks, including Orestes and Pylades, are brought to Iphigenia, who prepares them with lustration for sacrifice and questions the justice of human offerings.

l: the Erinnyes’ persecution of Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: After Orestes kills his mother to avenge his father, the avenging Erinyes drive him into exile and madness. His journey to Tauri is connected with his hope of relief from their persecution. After Orestes killed his mother, the Erinnyes pursued him through repeated wanderings and caused him to be regarded as frantic. Even after the trial, those who rejected its judgment continued driving him until he returned to Phoebus’s sanctuary.

l: escape of Iphigenia and Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The escape of Iphigenia and Orestes from Tauris is a flight by sea with the sacred image. Orestes and Pylades, captured near the temple, are freed when Iphigenia says they must be purified away from it. At the shore she releases them, boards the Grecian ship with Orestes and the image, and escapes despite Thoas's men and rough water, with Minerva ensuring success.

l: Argive family, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The Argive family is the royal house of Argos/Mycenae, associated with Pelops, Atreus, Agamemnon, Menelaus, Iphigenia, and Orestes. It suffers murders, deaths, separation, and lost authority; Iphigenia mourns its destruction and believes Orestes lost.

l: mourning for Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: is_performed_by Iphigenia [through funeral offerings] Iphigenia mourns Orestes after interpreting her dream as proof of his death. She prepares libations, wine, milk-like offerings, honey, and locks of her hair for his imagined funeral rites, while the Chorus sings a lament.

l: Greek sacrificial custom, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: differs_from human sacrifice [the Taurian practice is not hallowed among Greeks] The Greek practice of sacrifice is contrasted with the custom of the land where Iphigenia serves Artemis. Iphigenia says that the sacrifice offered there is not hallowed among the Greeks.

l: Orestes’ exile, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Orestes’ exile is his wandering after killing Clytemnestra: having left his homeland both unwillingly and willingly, he is nowhere and everywhere, traveling with Pylades until arriving in Tauris.

l: letter from Iphigenia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Iphigenia’s letter is a message for her friends in Argos, especially Orestes, carried by Pylades if he is spared. Beginning with her supposed death at Aulis, it reveals that Iphigenia survived because the Goddess substituted a hind, and insists that she did not willingly become a murderess. Written for a cenotaph at Mycenæ when she expected to die, it now asks Orestes to rescue her from the barbarian land before she dies. Iphigenia retrieves it from Artemis’ shrine to send it.

l: dreams of Orestes’ death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: mislead Iphigenia [she interprets them as Orestes' death] Iphigenia’s dreams led her to believe that Orestes no longer saw the sun. When Orestes reports that he is supposedly nowhere, she concludes that the dreams were meaningless.

l: Orestes’ supposed death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Iphigenia, guided by dreams and reports, believes Orestes dead; before recognizing the living stranger, his answers make her think no account of him remains.

l: Iphigenia’s slavery, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Iphigenia’s long-term captivity in Tauris keeps her serving Artemis in sacrificial duties; longing for Argos, she hopes a letter reaching Argive friends will end it.

l: sea voyage to Tauris, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: is_made_by Orestes [with Pylades] The Chorus describes the long voyage from Greece through dangerous waters to the inhospitable land. Orestes calls himself the steersman of the voyage that brought him and Pylades into their present troubles.

l: the planned sacrifice of Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The planned sacrifice of Orestes is to occur at Artemis's temple in barbarian land, where he is destined for ritual death by an Argive woman's hand and Iphigenia is to conduct the strangers' sacrifice. Iphigenia prevents it by pretending purification, leading the strangers to the shore, and helping them escape.

l: the oath concerning the letter, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: An oath binds Pylades to deliver Iphigenia's letter to her friends and Iphigenia to secure his escape. Pylades invokes Zeus, Iphigenia Artemis; after allowing for loss at sea, they ensure the message survives by having Pylades learn it by heart.

l: hind, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The hind is the animal that the Goddess gave in exchange for Iphigenia at the sacrifice. Agamemnon sacrificed it while believing that he was sacrificing Iphigenia.

l: the fate of Orestes and Pylades, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Orestes expects to die in the sacrifice, while Pylades initially declares that he will die with him rather than return alone. Their situation changes when Iphigenia recognizes Orestes as her brother and arranges for Pylades to carry her letter and help secure their escape.

l: the oracle’s command to seize the image, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: Phoebus’s oracle commands Orestes to come to the barbarian land, seize the heaven-sent image of Diana, and place it in Athens. Orestes believes that obeying this command will end his madness and allow him to return to Mycenae.

l: the escape plan, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: requires the ship [to carry Iphigenia, Orestes, Pylades, and the image away] Iphigenia will tell the king that Orestes and Pylades are polluted and cannot be sacrificed until they are purified at the sea. She will claim that the image was touched by them and must also be washed, then carry it to the ship herself while the others help preserve the secret.

l: purification, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: is_pretended_by Iphigenia [to enable the strangers' escape] Iphigenia claims that the strangers and the sacred image require purification because of the stain of matricide. She orders sea water, fire, lamps, lambs, fetters, and other ritual objects, but the purification is only a deception intended to conceal the escape.

l: voyage to Athens, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The voyage begins when Iphigenia, Orestes, and the sacred image board the Grecian ship. The ship is driven back by a strong tide and approaches the rocks, but Minerva commands the sea to become calm and directs the vessel toward Athens.

l: altar, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I
s: The altar appears as the place toward which victims are led for sacrifice. The notes also compare the play’s sacrificial altar with descriptions of ritual killing in other ancient sources.

The document presents Euripides’ Alcestis as a pro-satyric, pathetic comedy: a refinement of a broad comic Satyr-play tradition in which grief, blame, hospitality, and heroic rescue lead to rejoicing rather than conventional tragic finality. Apollo explains that Admetus escaped death because his wife Alcestis agreed to die for him, though Thanatos arrives to claim her. Alcestis, devoted but practical, bids farewell to Admetus and their children, secures his promise not to replace her with another wife or stepmother, and dies. The Chorus mourns the Daughter of Pelias as a model wife who died in another’s stead, while condemning Admetus’s aged parents for refusing to do so. Admetus, generous and affectionate yet selfish and self-deceiving, conceals Alcestis’s death when Heracles arrives, preserving hospitality even as the funeral proceeds. He later bitterly reproaches his father Pheres. Heracles, initially a feasting heroic reveller, learns the truth from a Servant, sobers, and resolves to recover Alcestis from Death. After Admetus returns home declaring life without her worse than death, Heracles brings a veiled woman and compels him to receive her. He reveals that he has wrested Alcestis from Death. Silent for the moment, she enters the restored household, while Heracles leaves for further labors and Admetus celebrates renewed happiness.

Alcestis is Euripides’ earliest dated surviving play, a pro-satyric fourth work replacing a Satyr-play. Its regular saga plot and tragic diction combine pathos, comedy, rejoicing, and slight epic or over-colloquial extravagance; Heracles supplies a Satyric or revelling presence, making its status as tragedy doubtful.

Euripides is a poet who wrote Alcestis, reshaping a traditional story through close psychological analysis into refined, pathetic comedy, delicately and sympathetically treating Alcestis while retaining faint satire or amusement.

Admetus is the king and ruler of Pherae in Thessaly, son of Pheres, husband of Alcestis, and father of their two children. He is portrayed as generous, hospitable, innocent, artistic, affectionate, eloquent, impulsive, and spoiled, yet also unconsciously insincere, self-blinded, and fundamentally selfish in accepting the sacrifice expected of others. When threatened with death, he is saved because Alcestis agrees to die in his place, while his mother and father refuse. After her death, he grieves intensely, orders mourning and funeral honors, promises never to remarry, accepts responsibility for their children, and maintains that a new bride would dishonor Alcestis and be hated by the children. Even while mourning, he conceals Alcestis's death from Heracles and receives him hospitably, refusing to turn away a guest. He quarrels violently with Pheres for not dying in his place, then collapses in grief. Returning to his empty house, he confronts the loss of Alcestis, his happiness, and his honor; public shame and self-judgment lead him to recognize what her sacrifice cost. Though he resists remarriage, he accepts a veiled woman at Heracles's insistence and discovers Alcestis restored to life, becoming again her husband and Heracles's acknowledged friend.

Alcestis is the beautiful, devoted, simple, homely, practical wife and queen of Admetus, daughter of Pelias, sister of Acastus, and mother of her and Admetus’s two children. An orphan raised in Admetus’s house, she is deeply loved by him and valued by the household, including servants she protected from his anger. Though not artistic, she has unconscious poetry; she is idealized without being merely blameless. What matters most is her courage and fidelity: alone among those able to do so, she gives her life in Admetus’s place to save him, without fearing death. Before dying, she makes him promise to care for their children and never remarry, fearing a stepmother might mistreat them. Her death has occurred as the main action begins. Minstrels, the chorus, and others praise her as a faithful, generous, noble wife, a queen of women, and a spouse of spouses; she is received by the underworld in another’s stead. Heracles then wins her back from Death. Veiled and resembling her former self, she returns to Admetus’s house but remains speechless for three days, until cleansing and purification are complete.

Heracles is a demi-god, Zeus-born son of Alcmena, a hero and figure of the Satyr world: boisterous, convivial, and especially suited to Satyr-play, yet also a tragic deliverer. Traveling through Pherae on the Argive King’s command to seize Diomede’s man-eating horses in Thrace, he arrives tired and is welcomed as Admetus’s guest. Unaware that Alcestis has died, he feasts, drinks, and sings amid the household’s concealed grief. Once a Servant tells him the truth, his revelling gives way to horror and resolve. To repay Admetus’s hospitality and as his friend, he goes among the dead, fights and wrestles Death, and returns Alcestis alive. Back at Admetus’s house, he first presents her as a woman won in contests, then reveals her identity, and departs to continue his quest rather than stay for a feast. He is portrayed as triumphant, kind, wise, and still marked by a mocking, Satyric spirit.

Satyr-play is a play performed after three tragedies, using traditional saga plots, heroic characters, tragic diction, and a Chorus of Satyrs to create controlled burlesque; it joins revelry, joy, nature, Dionysus, earth’s renewal, and resurrection.

is_a dramatic form [derived from Satyr-play] A pro-satyric drama is a stage in the refinement of the complete Satyr-play, retaining a normal chorus while including one Satyric or revelling figure. Alcestis is identified as a clear example because it has tragic diction, a traditional saga plot, and Heracles as its central revelling figure.

Satyrs are attendant daemons of Dionysus, forming his revel rout. Combining human or divine and animal features, especially horses or wild goats, they embody joyous, instinctive nature, drunken absurdity, and mysterious wild joy; ancient religion connects them with resurrection of the dead.
A deity compelled to serve Admetus protects him by delaying death, arranging a substitute, confronting Thanatos, predicting Heracles, and leaving before Alcestis dies.

Death is the headsman of the pit, a black, winged lord of corpses and Lord of the Dead who governs mortality and claims the dead. He comes to the Castle of Admetus to claim Alcestis as his destined prey, rejects Apollo's request to delay her death, and enters to place his drawn sword upon her. He holds Alcestis among the dead and binds Admetus to sorrow, but Heracles fights him, seizes him as he flees, and recovers Alcestis from his power.

Pheres is Admetus’s father, a free-born Thessalian of chiefly ancestry who owns Thessaly by inheritance and rule. He refuses to die to save Admetus. At Alcestis’s burial he brings gifts and praise, clashes with Admetus over that refusal, defends each person’s single life, and departs accusing Admetus of letting a woman die for him.

is_a city in Thessaly [ruled by Admetus] Pherae is the realm of Admetus, whose citizens and elders mourn Alcestis. Admetus orders the people of Pherae to wear mourning and forbids music and celebration for twelve moons.

is_a virtue [shown by sheltering strangers in grief] Admetus refuses to turn Heracles away from his house during the mourning and orders that he be given separate rooms, food, and drink. He regards welcoming a stranger as a duty and believes that preserving hospitality will make Heracles his friend rather than leave him friendless in a foreign land.

Alcestis’s sacrifice for Admetus is a self-sacrifice made so that he can escape death and preserve his life. When no one else will die in his place, she undertakes to die, giving up her youth and happiness because she cannot bear separation from Admetus and their children. She also seeks to protect the children by securing Admetus’s promise not to remarry. Afterward, Alcestis is remembered as brave and faithful, while Admetus regrets not dying with her.

Heracles’s contest with Death is a wrestling struggle to restore Alcestis to Admetus. After learning that she has died, Heracles vows to repay Admetus’s hospitality, planning to confront Death at the tomb or seek her return below. Among graves and the dead, he springs upon and grips Death as he flees, conquers him by force of combat, and brings Alcestis back from death.

l: the two children of Admetus and Alcestis, Alcestis
s: Admetus and Alcestis's children bid farewell as Alcestis leaves, are entrusted to Admetus, later loathe a new bride.

is_a son of Alcestis The little boy runs to Alcestis after she dies and asks why she has gone away, touching her face and calling to her. He tells Admetus that he and his little sister are lonely and cold without their mother.
Admetus’s handmaid tearfully reports Alcestis’s prayers, farewells, suffering, and impending death to the Chorus, then returns inside.

Chorus is a chorus of citizen elders of Pherae and friends of Admetus’s household. Outside Admetus’s castle, it fears and mourns Alcestis’s death, wishes but cannot save her, and praises her as a brave, true wife who died for her lover. It imagines lasting fame for her, condemns Admetus’s parents’ failure, and, after consoling Admetus, insists that Fate is irresistible and grief must be endured.

is_a house of the dead [the realm to which the dead go] Hades is described as the realm beneath the earth to which Thanatos takes the dead. Alcestis imagines the boat and Ferryman of the Dead carrying her toward its palaces.

is_a ancient castle near Pherae [the setting of the play] The Castle of Admetus is the setting for Alcestis's final preparations, death, and mourning. Apollo watches it, Thanatos enters it to claim Alcestis, and her body is carried from it for burial.

Alcestis’s death is a voluntary substitution undertaken in place of Admetus, saving him. After giving final instructions and farewells to Admetus and their children, she dies and goes alone to the hungry dead. Her death overwhelms Admetus, the children, the Handmaid, the Servant, and the Chorus with grief; Admetus conceals it from Heracles, feels shame, rejects entering his house, and will not accept another wife. The Chorus celebrates her courage and love as worthy of lasting song, fame, and blessing.
Admetus's bargain with Death spares his life if another living soul dies; after his parents refuse, Alcestis fulfills it by sacrificing her life.

Alcestis’s funeral and burial is an honorable, publicly mourned rite ordered by Admetus throughout Thessaly. After her death, mourners carry her body into the house; later, a procession bears it on a bier toward a grave-mound near the Larissa road and a burial urn. Citizens farewell her, and Pheres provides burial gifts.

is_required_for Alcestis's funeral and burial [throughout Admetus's realm] Grief fills the Castle of Admetus as Admetus, the children, the Handmaid, the servants, and the Chorus respond to Alcestis's death. Admetus orders mourning throughout Pherae, including mourning clothes, shorn horse manes, and the silence of musical instruments for twelve moons.
Admetus’s home is desolate after Alcestis’s death, confronting him with her absence; when Alcestis returns, he leads her inside and declares its fortune renewed.
Sunless Houses is the underworld, a dark realm of tears and hungry dead, where a cold grey-handed guide carries shadows across the Tears that Well through night and water.
Marriage and conjugal devotion is a rare lifelong unity, exemplified as Alcestis, Pelias’s daughter, dies for her lord, showing two hearts remain one-knit forever.

A slave attendant in Admetus's household, the Servant serves its hospitality and loves Alcestis like a mother. While obeying orders to conceal mourning from Heracles, the Servant angrily reveals Alcestis's death and grieves her loss.

is_a unavoidable human condition [every mortal must face it] Heracles tells the Servant that every mortal must pay the debt of death and cannot know whether life will last another day. The quarrel between Admetus and Pheres shows their conflicting attitudes toward mortality: Admetus condemns Pheres for clinging to life, while Pheres insists that his own life is as precious to him as Admetus's is to Admetus.
Fate is an irresistible power controlling life and death; from an empty stage, its unbreakable grip is shown beyond Zeus, ritual, philosophy, medicine, or magic.

is_a Alcestis [initially veiled and unrecognized] The veiled woman is presented by Heracles as a prize won through dangerous contests and is initially intended to become an attendant in Admetus’s house. When unveiled, she is revealed to be Alcestis, not a stranger.

is_brought_about_by Heracles [after his combat with Death] Alcestis returns from the realm of the dead through Heracles’s intervention. She remains silent at first and is taken home to Admetus, who recognizes and embraces the hope of having her again.

concerns Alcestis's death [as enduring bereavement] Admetus sees his life without Alcestis as worse than death and imagines enduring loneliness, reproach, and the empty household. His grief briefly deepens when the veiled woman resembles Alcestis, but it changes to astonishment and joy when she is revealed.

governs Admetus [in his judgment of remarriage and survival] Admetus fears that people will call him shameful for allowing Alcestis to die in his place and for continuing to live. He insists that remaining unmarried will honor her, and the Chorus holds that Alcestis’s sacrifice deserves lasting honor.

are_contrasted_by Admetus [through Alcestis's death and return] Admetus initially prefers death to a life emptied of Alcestis, while the Chorus insists that human beings must endure what Fate brings. Heracles’s victory over Death transforms the situation, restoring Alcestis to life and renewing Admetus’s faith in Fortune.

s: the two children of Jason and Medea are children of Jason (their father's children)
q: your father never has forgot Your needs

s: the two children of Jason and Medea carry poisoned gifts (to the royal bride)
q: Come, children, lift With heed these caskets. Bear them as your gift To her, being bride and princess and of right Blessed

s: the Chorus of Corinthian Women is a chorus (the collective singing group)
q: CHORUS.

s: Medea is mother of the two children of Jason and Medea (their mother)
q: I was their mother!

s: the Chorus of Corinthian Women knows about the killing of Medea's children (and believes it is imminent)
q: Now I have no hope more of the children's living; No hope more. They are gone forth unto death

s: the Chorus of Corinthian Women pleads against the killing of Medea's children (through the women’s warning and prayer)
q: Every side, Every way, Lo, we kneel to thee and pray: By thy knees, by thy soul, O woman wild! One at least thou canst not slay, Not thy child

s: the Leader admonishes Medea (against the planned deed)
q: I, loving thee, and helping in their need Man's laws, adjure thee, dream not of this deed

s: the Nurse works these high services
q: Ho, woman; get thee gone And lead lord Jason hither. . . . There is none Like thee, to work me these high services

s: Jason's new bride accepts poisoned gifts (as a bride and princess)
q: The royal bride hath mildly bent Her hand to accept thy gifts

s: Jason's new bride is target of the killing of the royal bride (through the poisoned robe and crown)
q: The bride, she taketh the poison of their giving: She taketh the bounden gold and openeth; And the crown, the crown, she lifteth about her brow

s: poisoned gifts include the poison (the robe and wreath are poisoned)
q: Such poison shall they drink, my robe and wreath!

s: poisoned gifts includes Fine robings and a carcanet of gold
q: Fine robings and a carcanet of gold

s: Medea is married to Jason (in a marriage-bed she regards as betrayed)
q: Why must thou to-day Turn strange, and make thee like some evil thing, Childish, to meet my childish passioning

s: the marriage-bed is of Medea
q: How his will now is my will, how all things Are well, touching this marriage-bed of kings For which I am

s: the Sun is ancestor of Medea (through her house)
q: Being wed with thee, the bravest of the brave, And girt with raiment which of old the sire Of all my house, the Sun, gave, steeped in fire, To his own fiery race

s: Aegeus has a gentle and a righteous heart
q: Our eyes have seen thee as thou art, A gentle and a righteous heart

s: Maia's guiding Son guides Aegeus (on his return to his hearth and fire)
q: Farewell: and Maia's guiding Son Back lead thee to thy hearth and fire, Aegeus

s: Athens is a walled hill (the place where Medea hopes to escape)
q: In Athens' walled hill.

s: Corinth is the place of Medea's exile (the city from which Medea is cast out)
q: Seeing it is the king's behest To cast me out from Corinth

s: Medea is in Medea's exile (as a person condemned to leave Corinth)
q: Seeing it is the king's behest To cast me out from Corinth . . . aye, and best, Far best, for me--I know it--not to stay Longer to trouble thee and those who sway The realm

s: Medea seeks refuge in Athens (to escape her enemies and exile)
q: Here will I make fast Mine anchor, and escape them at the last In Athens' walled hill

s: Medea regards as friend Aegeus (as a source of refuge and power)
q: Here at my worst hour A friend is found, a very port of power To save my shipwreck
